questiontext.text: In a cause-effect graph, what is a cause?

answer.text: A distinct input condition (something that can be true or false) drawn from the specification

feedback.text: Correct — a cause is an individual input condition, evaluated as true or false.

answer.text: An output or action the program produces

feedback.text: That is an effect, not a cause.

answer.text: A line of source code that must be executed

feedback.text: Cause-effect graphing is black-box; causes come from the specification, not the code.

answer.text: A column of the resulting decision table

feedback.text: A column is a rule/test case derived later; a cause is an input condition.

generalfeedback.text: A cause is a distinct input condition — a boolean that can hold or not hold. Causes are identified by reading the specification and are wired through boolean nodes to the effects they influence.

questiontext.text: In a cause-effect graph, what is an effect?

answer.text: An output condition or action the system produces in response to its inputs

feedback.text: Correct — effects are the observable outputs/actions on the right of the graph.

answer.text: An input condition that can be true or false

feedback.text: That describes a cause, not an effect.
Constraints (E/I/O/R) restrict causes; an effect is an output.

answer.text: A boolean operator node such as AND or OR

feedback.text: Those nodes wire causes to effects; the effect itself is the output.

generalfeedback.text: An effect is an output condition or action. In the graph, causes on the left are connected through boolean nodes to effects on the right, and each effect is ultimately true or false for a given cause assignment.

questiontext.text: What does an IDENTITY node mean when it connects a cause to an effect?

answer.text: The effect is true exactly when the single cause is true (it copies the cause's value)

feedback.text: Correct — identity passes the cause value straight through to the effect.

answer.text: The effect is true exactly when the cause is false

feedback.text: That is the NOT node, not identity.

answer.text: The effect is true when either of two causes is true

feedback.text: That is an OR node; identity connects a single cause.

answer.text: The effect is always true regardless of the cause

feedback.text: Identity mirrors the cause; it is not a constant-true node.

generalfeedback.text: An IDENTITY node ties one cause to one effect so that effect = cause: if the cause is true the effect is true, and if the cause is false the effect is false.

questiontext.text: What does a NOT (~) node compute?

answer.text: The effect is true exactly when its single cause is false (it negates the cause)

feedback.text: Correct — NOT inverts the cause value.

answer.text: The effect is true exactly when the cause is true

feedback.text: That is IDENTITY; NOT gives the opposite.

answer.text: The effect is true when all of several causes are true

feedback.text: That is AND; NOT takes a single cause and negates it.

answer.text: The effect is true when at least one of several causes is true

feedback.text: That is OR; NOT negates one cause.

generalfeedback.text: A NOT node (drawn ~) negates: the effect is true when the cause is false and false when the cause is true.

questiontext.text: What does an AND (∧) node compute for an effect wired to several causes?

answer.text: The effect is true only when every one of the connected causes is true

feedback.text: Correct — AND requires all inputs true.

answer.text: The effect is true when at least one connected cause is true

feedback.text: That is OR, not AND.

answer.text: The effect is true when exactly one connected cause is true

feedback.text: AND requires all of them, not exactly one.

answer.text: The effect copies the value of the first cause only

feedback.text: AND depends on every input, not just the first.

generalfeedback.text: An AND node yields true only when all its input causes (or intermediate nodes) are true; if any input is false, the effect is false.

questiontext.text: What does an OR (∨) node compute for an effect wired to several causes?

answer.text: The effect is true when at least one of the connected causes is true

feedback.text: Correct — OR needs only one true input.

answer.text: The effect is true only when all connected causes are true

feedback.text: That is AND, not OR.

answer.text: The effect is true only when exactly one connected cause is true

feedback.text: OR is true for one or more; "exactly one" is a different (O) idea.

answer.text: The effect is true only when all connected causes are false

feedback.text: That would be a NOR (NOT of an OR); a plain OR is true when any input is true.

generalfeedback.text: An OR node yields true when one or more of its inputs is true, and false only when every input is false.

questiontext.text: Among a set of causes, the Exclusive (E) constraint means what?

answer.text: At most one of the causes may be true (they can all be false, but no two are true together)

feedback.text: Correct — E allows zero or one true, never two or more.

answer.text: Exactly one of the causes must be true

feedback.text: That is the One-and-only-one (O) constraint; E also permits all false.

answer.text: At least one of the causes must be true

feedback.text: That is the Inclusive (I) constraint.

answer.text: All of the causes must be true together

feedback.text: E forbids two being true at once, so it can never require all true.

generalfeedback.text: Exclusive (E): at most one of the constrained causes is true. Zero true is allowed; two or more true is forbidden.

questiontext.text: Among a set of causes, the Inclusive (I) constraint means what?

answer.text: At least one of the causes must be true (they cannot all be false)

feedback.text: Correct — I forbids the all-false case; one or more must hold.

answer.text: At most one of the causes may be true

feedback.text: That is the Exclusive (E) constraint.

answer.text: Exactly one of the causes must be true

feedback.text: That is the One-and-only-one (O) constraint; I allows several to be true.

answer.text: The causes have no restriction at all

feedback.text: I does restrict them: it rules out all being false.

generalfeedback.text: Inclusive (I): at least one of the constrained causes must be true. Any number from one up to all is allowed; only all-false is forbidden.

questiontext.text: Among a set of causes, the One-and-only-one (O) constraint means what?

answer.text: Exactly one of the causes is true — no more, no fewer

feedback.text: Correct — O requires precisely one true.

answer.text: At most one of the causes may be true (all-false allowed)

feedback.text: That is Exclusive (E); O forbids the all-false case.

answer.text: At least one of the causes must be true

feedback.text: That is Inclusive (I), which also allows several true; O allows only one.

answer.text: Either all or none of the causes are true

feedback.text: O requires exactly one true, not all-or-none.

generalfeedback.text: One-and-only-one (O): exactly one of the constrained causes is true. It is the combination of Exclusive (at most one) and Inclusive (at least one).

questiontext.text: The Requires (R) constraint "cause a Requires cause b" means what?

answer.text: Whenever a is true, b must also be true (so a=true with b=false is impossible)

feedback.text: Correct — R rules out the a-true, b-false combination.

answer.text: Whenever a is true, b must be false

feedback.text: That is the opposite; R forces b true when a is true.

answer.text: a and b must always have the same value

feedback.text: R is one-directional: b may be true while a is false; only a-true-b-false is forbidden.

answer.text: Exactly one of a and b may be true

feedback.text: That is closer to Exclusive/One-and-only-one; R is an implication a→b.

generalfeedback.text: Requires (R) is the implication a→b: if a is true then b must be true. The only forbidden combination is a=true, b=false; all others (including a=false with any b) are allowed.

questiontext.text: The Masks (M) constraint "effect a Masks effect b" means what?

answer.text: If effect a occurs (is true), then effect b is masked and forced to be false

feedback.text: Correct — M is a constraint among effects: a true suppresses b.

answer.text: If cause a is true, cause b must be true

feedback.text: That is Requires (R), a constraint among causes; M constrains effects.

answer.text: At most one of effects a and b may occur, but either may occur alone

feedback.text: M is directional — a suppresses b, but b does not suppress a — so it is not a symmetric "at most one".

answer.text: Effects a and b must always occur together

feedback.text: M does the opposite: when a occurs, b cannot.

generalfeedback.text: Masks (M) is the one constraint that applies among effects rather than causes: when effect a is true, effect b is masked (forced false), regardless of what the graph would otherwise compute for b.

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired to a single cause by an IDENTITY node:

E = IDENTITY(c1)

If c1 = true, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — identity copies the cause, so E = c1 = true.
Identity does not invert; E equals c1, which is true.

answer.text: Undefined — an effect needs at least two causes

feedback.text: An identity node connects exactly one cause to the effect; that is valid.

answer.text: It depends on other causes not shown

feedback.text: The effect is wired only to c1 via identity, so only c1 matters.

generalfeedback.text: IDENTITY passes the cause straight through: E = c1. With c1 = true, E = true.

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired to a single cause by a NOT node:

E = ~c1

If c1 = false, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — NOT inverts: ~false = true.
NOT negates the cause; with c1 false, E is true.
A NOT node takes a single cause; the effect is well defined.
That would be identity; NOT gives the opposite of c1.

generalfeedback.text: A NOT node gives E = ~c1. With c1 = false, E = ~false = true.

questiontext.text: Cause-effect graphing is a black-box (specification-based) test-design technique.

feedback.text: Correct — it derives tests from the specification's input conditions and outputs, not from the source code.
Causes and effects are read from the specification, so the technique is black-box, not structural.

generalfeedback.text: Cause-effect graphing identifies input conditions (causes) and outputs (effects) from the specification and wires them with boolean logic — a black-box technique, independent of the code's internal structure.

questiontext.text: Four of the five constraint types (E, I, O, R, M) restrict combinations of causes. Which one instead restricts effects?

feedback.text: Correct — Masks is the effect-side constraint; E, I, O, R all restrict causes.
E restricts causes (at most one true), not effects.
R restricts causes (a→b), not effects.
O restricts causes (exactly one true), not effects.

generalfeedback.text: E, I, O, and R express relationships among causes (inputs). M (Masks) is the only one that relates two effects: if the first occurs, it forces the second to be false.

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired as:

E = c1 ∧ c2

Given c1 = true, c2 = false, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — AND needs both true; c2 is false, so E is false.
AND requires every input true; c2 = false forces E false.
Both inputs are given, so E is well defined.
E depends on both causes; with c2 false the AND is false regardless of c1.

generalfeedback.text: E = c1 ∧ c2 = true ∧ false = false. An AND is true only when all inputs are true.

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired as:

E = c1 ∨ c2

Given c1 = false, c2 = true, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — OR is true when any input is true; c2 is true.
OR needs only one true input, and c2 is true.
Both inputs are given, so E is well defined.
E depends on both; c2 being true makes the OR true.

generalfeedback.text: E = c1 ∨ c2 = false ∨ true = true. An OR is false only when every input is false.

name.text: Evaluate AND with a negated input

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired as:

E = c1 ∧ ~c2

Given c1 = true, c2 = false, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — ~c2 = true and c1 = true, so the AND is true.
Since c2 is false, ~c2 is true, and true ∧ true = true.
Both causes are given, so E is well defined.
E uses ~c2, and combined with c1 it evaluates to true here.

generalfeedback.text: First negate: ~c2 = ~false = true. Then E = c1 ∧ ~c2 = true ∧ true = true.

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired as:

E = c1 ∨ c2 ∨ c3

Given c1 = false, c2 = false, c3 = false, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — an OR is false only when every input is false, which is the case here.
All three inputs are false, so the OR is false.
All inputs are given; E is well defined.
No constraint is stated; the OR of three falses is simply false.

generalfeedback.text: E = false ∨ false ∨ false = false. An OR yields false precisely when all inputs are false.

name.text: Model "at most one" with a constraint

questiontext.text: A spec says: "At most one of the three coupon codes may be applied to an order (applying none is allowed)." Which constraint models this among the three cause inputs?

feedback.text: Correct — "at most one, none allowed" is exactly Exclusive.
O would force exactly one to be applied; here applying none is allowed, so it is E.
I requires at least one true; here zero is allowed, so it is E.
R is an implication between two specific causes, not an "at most one of a set" rule.

generalfeedback.text: "At most one may be true, and all-false is allowed" is the Exclusive (E) constraint. If the spec had forbidden all-false, it would be One-and-only-one (O).

name.text: Model "at least one" with a constraint

questiontext.text: A spec says: "At least one contact method (phone, email, or address) must be provided." Which constraint models this among the three cause inputs?

feedback.text: Correct — "at least one" is exactly the Inclusive constraint.
E means at most one; here we need one or more, which is I.
O means exactly one; here providing several is fine, so it is I.
M is an effect constraint, not a rule about how many causes are true.

generalfeedback.text: "At least one must be true" is the Inclusive (I) constraint; it forbids only the all-false case.

questiontext.text: A spec says: "Exactly one payment method — cash, card, or voucher — must be selected." Which constraint models this among the three cause inputs?

feedback.text: Correct — "exactly one" is the One-and-only-one constraint.
E allows zero true; here one must always be selected, so it is O.
I allows several true; here only one may be selected, so it is O.
R is an a→b implication, not a "select exactly one of a set" rule.

generalfeedback.text: "Exactly one true" combines Exclusive (at most one) and Inclusive (at least one): that is the One-and-only-one (O) constraint.

questiontext.text: A spec says: "Selecting express shipping requires that a delivery address has been entered." Which constraint models this?

feedback.text: Correct — one cause being true forces another to be true.
The spec is not "exactly one of the two"; it is an implication a→b, i.e. R.
E forbids both being true; here both true is exactly the intended, valid case.
M relates effects; this rule relates two input causes, so it is R.

generalfeedback.text: "a requires b" is the Requires (R) constraint, the implication a→b: express-shipping true forces delivery-address true, ruling out express-shipping with no address.

questiontext.text: Why do we build a cause-effect graph and then convert it to a decision table, rather than testing every input combination?

answer.text: The graph's logic and constraints let us derive only the feasible, behaviour-relevant combinations, yielding a manageable set of tests instead of all 2^n

feedback.text: Correct — that systematic reduction to meaningful combinations is the whole point.

answer.text: It guarantees 100% statement and branch coverage of the code

feedback.text: Cause-effect graphing is black-box; it targets input-combination logic, not code-coverage metrics.

answer.text: It removes the need to specify expected outputs

feedback.text: Each rule/column still carries the expected effect; the technique does not drop the oracle.

answer.text: It makes exhaustive testing of all 2^n combinations faster to run

feedback.text: The goal is to avoid exhaustive testing, keeping only the feasible, distinct combinations.

generalfeedback.text: Testing all 2^n cause combinations is usually infeasible. The graph captures the logic and constraints, and tracing effects back yields a decision table whose columns are the feasible, distinct combinations — a systematic, manageable test set.

questiontext.text: Spec: "A withdrawal is allowed if the card is valid, the PIN is correct, and the balance is sufficient; otherwise the transaction is declined and, if the PIN is wrong three times, the card is retained." How many distinct causes does this spec suggest?

answer.text: 4 — card valid, PIN correct, balance sufficient, PIN wrong three times

feedback.text: Correct — these are the four distinct input conditions.

answer.text: 3 — card valid, PIN correct, balance sufficient

feedback.text: "PIN wrong three times" is a fourth distinct input condition.
"Allowed" and "declined" are effects (outputs), not causes.
Only distinct input conditions are causes; not every noun qualifies.

generalfeedback.text: Causes are the distinct input conditions: card valid, PIN correct, balance sufficient, and PIN wrong three times — four causes. "Allowed", "declined", and "retained" are effects.

questiontext.text: Using the same ATM spec — "…the transaction is allowed or declined, and the card may be retained" — how many distinct effects are there?

feedback.text: Correct — those are the three distinct output conditions/actions.
"Card retained" is a third distinct effect.

answer.text: 4 — the same as the number of causes

feedback.text: Causes and effects are counted separately; there are three effects here.
There are three distinct outputs, not one.

generalfeedback.text: Effects are the distinct outputs/actions: allowed, declined, and card retained — three effects. Counting causes and effects is the first step of building the graph.

name.text: Evaluate an OR feeding an AND

questiontext.text:
The graph has an intermediate node and an effect:

n1 = c1 ∨ c2
E  = n1 ∧ c3

Given c1 = false, c2 = true, c3 = true, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — n1 = false ∨ true = true, then E = true ∧ true = true.
n1 is true (c2), and c3 is true, so the AND is true.
All causes are given, so E is well defined.
E depends on the OR of c1,c2 and on c3, not on c1 alone.

generalfeedback.text: Evaluate the intermediate node first: n1 = c1 ∨ c2 = false ∨ true = true. Then E = n1 ∧ c3 = true ∧ true = true.

questiontext.text: A spec says: "When the 'account locked' error is shown, the 'welcome' message must not be shown." Which constraint captures this relationship between the two outputs?

answer.text: M (Masks): the account-locked effect masks the welcome effect

feedback.text: Correct — one effect occurring forces the other to be suppressed, which is Masks.
These are outputs, not causes; the effect-side constraint is M.
R relates causes; here two effects are related, so it is M.
O constrains causes; this rule constrains effects, so it is M.

generalfeedback.text: A relationship that suppresses one output when another occurs is the Masks (M) constraint — the only constraint expressed among effects.

questiontext.text:
An effect is wired as:

E = ~(c1 ∨ c2)

Given c1 = false, c2 = false, what is E?

feedback.text: Correct — c1 ∨ c2 = false, and ~false = true.
The OR of two falses is false, and its negation is true.
Both causes are given, so E is well defined.
The NOT node inverts the OR, so E is the opposite of c1 ∨ c2.

generalfeedback.text: Evaluate inside first: c1 ∨ c2 = false ∨ false = false. Then negate: E = ~false = true. This "true only when all inputs are false" pattern is a NOR.

name.text: O versus E on the all-false case

questiontext.text: Two specs restrict the same set of causes. Spec 1: "select exactly one." Spec 2: "select at most one." What is the one difference between the constraints they imply?

answer.text: Spec 1 is O (all-false forbidden); Spec 2 is E (all-false allowed) — they differ only on whether zero-true is feasible

feedback.text: Correct — O and E agree except that O forbids the all-false combination.
They differ on the all-false case: O forbids it, E allows it.

answer.text: Spec 1 is I and Spec 2 is O

feedback.text: "Exactly one" is O and "at most one" is E; neither is Inclusive here.

answer.text: Spec 2 allows two true while Spec 1 does not

feedback.text: Both forbid two-or-more true; the only difference is the all-false case.

generalfeedback.text: One-and-only-one (O) = exactly one true; Exclusive (E) = at most one true. Both forbid two or more true; they differ solely in that E permits the all-false combination and O does not. Hence O has one fewer feasible combination than E for the same causes.

questiontext.text: Three causes c1, c2, c3 are governed by a One-and-only-one (O) constraint. Of the 2^3 = 8 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — exactly one true means one of {c1}, {c2}, {c3}: 3 feasible assignments.
4 would be the count under Exclusive (which also allows all-false); O forbids all-false, leaving 3.
7 is the Inclusive count (at least one true); O requires exactly one, giving 3.
There are three different ways for exactly one cause to be the true one, so 3.

generalfeedback.text: Under O exactly one cause is true. Enumerating the 8 assignments, only TFF, FTF, FFT qualify — 3 feasible combinations.

questiontext.text: Three causes c1, c2, c3 are governed by an Exclusive (E) constraint. Of the 8 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — at most one true: all-false plus the three single-true assignments = 4.
3 is the One-and-only-one count; E additionally allows the all-false case, giving 4.
7 is the Inclusive count; E is "at most one", which yields 4.
Enumerating "at most one true" gives FFF, TFF, FTF, FFT — 4, not 5.

generalfeedback.text: Under E at most one cause is true. Feasible: FFF, TFF, FTF, FFT — 4 combinations (one more than O, because all-false is allowed).

questiontext.text: Three causes c1, c2, c3 are governed by an Inclusive (I) constraint. Of the 8 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — at least one true rules out only the all-false case: 8 − 1 = 7.
I forbids the all-false assignment, so 7 (not all 8) remain.
3 is the One-and-only-one count; Inclusive allows any number ≥ 1 true, giving 7.
4 is the Exclusive count; Inclusive is "at least one", which gives 7.

generalfeedback.text: Under I at least one cause is true, so only FFF is forbidden. That leaves 8 − 1 = 7 feasible combinations.

questiontext.text: Two causes c1, c2 are governed by an Exclusive (E) constraint. Of the 2^2 = 4 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — at most one true: FF, TF, FT are feasible; only TT is ruled out.
2 is the One-and-only-one count; E also allows FF, giving 3.
E forbids both true (TT), so only 3 of the 4 remain.
Three assignments have at most one true, so 3 are feasible.

generalfeedback.text: Under E at most one of two causes is true, so TT is infeasible. Feasible: FF, TF, FT — 3 combinations.

questiontext.text: Four causes are governed by a One-and-only-one (O) constraint. Of the 2^4 = 16 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — exactly one true, and there are 4 choices of which cause is the true one.
5 would include the all-false case (that is Exclusive); O forbids all-false, leaving 4.
15 is the Inclusive count (at least one true); O requires exactly one, giving 4.
Any one of the four causes may be the single true one, so 4.

generalfeedback.text: Under O exactly one of the four causes is true, so the feasible assignments are TFFF, FTFF, FFTF, FFFT — 4 in all.

questiontext.text: Two causes a, b have the constraint a Requires b (a→b). Of the 4 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — only a=true, b=false is forbidden; the other 3 are feasible.
Only one assignment is ruled out, not three; 3 remain feasible.
The combination a=true, b=false violates a→b, so only 3 are feasible.
R rules out exactly one combination (a-true, b-false), leaving 3.

generalfeedback.text: a→b forbids only (a=true, b=false). The feasible assignments are (F,F), (F,T), (T,T) — 3 combinations.

questiontext.text: Three causes a, b, c have the single constraint a Requires b (a→b); c is unconstrained. Of the 2^3 = 8 assignments, how many are feasible?

feedback.text: Correct — a=true with b=false is forbidden for either value of c, removing 2 of the 8.
Two assignments are removed (a=T, b=F with c=F and with c=T), not one, so 6 remain.
Only the a-true, b-false cases are infeasible; that is 2 assignments, leaving 6.
c is free, so 6 assignments satisfy a→b, not 3.

generalfeedback.text: a→b forbids a=true, b=false. With c free, that pattern occurs for c=false and c=true — 2 infeasible assignments. So 8 − 2 = 6 are feasible.

name.text: Is a combination feasible under O

questiontext.text: Causes c1, c2, c3 are under a One-and-only-one (O) constraint. Is the assignment c1 = true, c2 = true, c3 = false feasible?

answer.text: No — two causes are true, but O allows exactly one true

feedback.text: Correct — with c1 and c2 both true, the O constraint is violated, so this column is infeasible.

answer.text: Yes — at least one cause is true

feedback.text: "At least one" is the Inclusive constraint; O demands exactly one, and here two are true.

answer.text: Yes — c3 is false, satisfying the constraint

feedback.text: O counts how many are true overall; two true (c1, c2) violates it regardless of c3.

answer.text: No — because c3 must be true

feedback.text: O does not require c3 specifically; it fails here simply because two causes are true.

generalfeedback.text: Under O exactly one cause may be true. Here c1 and c2 are both true, so the assignment is infeasible and yields no test case.

name.text: Effect value under the Masks constraint

questiontext.text: Two effects are computed from the graph, and effect A Masks effect B. For some input the graph gives A = true and would give B = true. After applying the Masks constraint, what are the observed effect values?

answer.text: A = true, B = false — because A occurs, B is masked (forced false)

feedback.text: Correct — Masks forces the second effect false whenever the first occurs.

answer.text: A = true, B = true — Masks does not change computed values

feedback.text: Masks specifically overrides B: when A is true, B is forced false.

answer.text: A = false, B = true — B masks A

feedback.text: The direction is A masks B, so A stays true and B is suppressed.

answer.text: Both false — a mask cancels both effects

feedback.text: Only the masked effect (B) is forced false; A remains as computed (true).

generalfeedback.text: Masks is directional: when the masking effect A is true, the masked effect B is forced to false, overriding whatever the graph computed for B. A itself is unaffected, so the result is A = true, B = false.

questiontext.text: An effect is E = c1 ∧ c2 with no constraints. Tracing back, how many cause assignments (the effect's "true points") make E true?

feedback.text: Correct — an AND is true for exactly the all-true assignment.
That describes an OR; an AND is true only when both are true.
c1 true with c2 false gives E false, so not every c1-true case counts.
E is false whenever either cause is false, so not all 4 assignments are true points.

generalfeedback.text: Tracing back from E = c1 ∧ c2, the only assignment that makes it true is (T, T). So the effect has a single true point, which becomes one decision-table column that fires E.

questiontext.text: An effect is E = c1 ∨ c2 with no constraints. How many cause assignments make E true?

feedback.text: Correct — an OR is true for every assignment except all-false.
That is the AND case; an OR needs only one true input.
(T,T) also makes an OR true, so there are 3 true points, not 2.
(F,F) makes the OR false, so only 3 assignments are true points.

generalfeedback.text: E = c1 ∨ c2 is true for (T,T), (T,F), (F,T) and false only for (F,F). That is 3 true points.

questiontext.text: A cause-effect graph has 3 causes under a One-and-only-one (O) constraint. If the decision table has one column per feasible cause combination, how many columns (and therefore test cases) does it have?

answer.text: 3 — one per feasible combination (exactly one cause true)

feedback.text: Correct — O leaves 3 feasible combinations, so 3 columns and 3 tests.
The O constraint removes the infeasible combinations; only 3 remain.
Under O the all-false case is not allowed, so it is 3, not 4.
Each feasible combination is a distinct column; there are 3.

generalfeedback.text: Building the decision table, each feasible cause combination becomes one column and thus one test case. With 3 causes under O there are 3 feasible combinations, giving 3 columns.

name.text: Infeasible combinations removed by E (3 causes)

questiontext.text: Three causes are governed by an Exclusive (E) constraint. How many of the 2^3 = 8 raw combinations become infeasible?

answer.text: 4 — the combinations with two or more causes true

feedback.text: Correct — 8 total minus 4 feasible (at most one true) = 4 infeasible.

name.text: Effect value across all feasible O columns

answer.text: 3 — in every feasible column, since exactly one cause is always true

feedback.text: Correct — O guarantees one cause is true, so the OR is true in all 3 feasible columns.
